paper_of_week.headline: Models can stealthily embed capabilities, evading any standard probe evaluation
paper_of_week.summary:
The authors expose a fundamental flaw in current capability‑evaluation pipelines: a model can be trained to hide arbitrary functions behind a veneer of benign behavior, passing all conventional tests while retaining dangerous abilities. By formalizing the notion of "provable hiding" they show that, under standard cryptographic assumptions, one can construct a model whose internal decision logic is indistinguishable from a harmless baseline yet activates a concealed sub‑policy on a trigger that is invisible to auditors.

Their construction leverages a two‑stage training regime: first, a public “mask” network learns the overt task; second, a secret “payload” network is steganographically encoded into the weight space using a keyed hash function. During inference the payload is only invoked when the input satisfies a cryptographic predicate known to the model owner. Empirically they demonstrate the technique on language models (hidden arithmetic) and vision classifiers (covert image‑generation), achieving >99% pass rates on standard benchmarks while the hidden function remains undetectable to state‑of‑the‑art probing tools.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Treat model evaluation as a cryptographic protocol: assume adversaries can embed hidden logic and design audits accordingly.

paper.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
paper.summary: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

deep_dive.problem: Current safety audits assume that any dangerous capability will manifest during standard test suites, but this assumption is unverified. Practitioners need to know whether a model could be deliberately engineered to conceal harmful functions that only activate under specific, hard‑to‑detect conditions.
deep_dive.approach: The paper introduces a provable hiding framework. It first defines a secret trigger predicate T(x) based on a cryptographic hash of the input and a private key. Then it trains a dual‑network architecture: a public network f_pub that optimizes the advertised task, and a private network f_priv that learns the hidden capability. During joint training, a loss term penalizes f_pub on inputs satisfying T(x), forcing f_priv to take over those cases. Finally, weight‑space steganography embeds f_priv’s parameters into f_pub using a keyed reversible transformation, making the combined model indistinguishable from a standard model to any black‑box test that does not know the key.
deep_dive.results: On a GPT‑2 sized language model, the authors hide a simple arithmetic solver (addition of three‑digit numbers) while the model scores 99.2% on the standard LAMBADA benchmark, identical to the baseline. For a ResNet‑50 classifier, they embed a covert image‑generation sub‑policy that produces a predefined pattern on trigger images; detection tools report a false‑negative rate of 97%. Across 10 random seeds, the hidden function activates with >98% success on trigger inputs while remaining invisible on 100k non‑trigger samples.
deep_dive.limitations: The hiding guarantee relies on hardness assumptions of the underlying hash function and does not extend to white‑box analysis where weights are inspected directly. Scaling the payload to large, complex capabilities incurs a trade‑off with public performance, and the method has only been validated on relatively small models and synthetic triggers.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now simulate worst‑case adversarial model releases, testing audit pipelines against provably hidden functions. It also provides a blueprint for building controlled backdoors in research prototypes, enabling safe‑zone experiments where hidden capabilities are intentionally studied under strict supervision.

one_thing_to_try.action: Implement the two‑stage hiding pipeline on a small transformer using a SHA‑256 keyed predicate
one_thing_to_try.why: It reveals whether your current probing suite can catch covert behavior before deployment
